_metadata.independence: I read only u01-blind-input.json; no other file under data/unlimited, no author text, no repository search, no web or API lookup was used, and all judgements rest on my own general knowledge.
_metadata.correction: v2 under the owner's corrected rubric relayed 2026-10-17: no minimum hint count, no board competition, generic allowed when natural to both words, compounds judged as compounds

hints.reason: The stock phrase 'king of the jungle' names the lion; KING is reached through that same idiom, which is universal.
A throne is a king's seat; lions reach it only via heraldry or Pride Rock in The Lion King, which needs explaining.
A mane is the lion's defining feature; nothing about it points to a king.
Lions roar; kings do not, and no idiom or compound bridges the gap.
Crown is the king's emblem; the crowned heraldic lion (as on the English royal arms) is a stretch for most players.
Aslan the lion is Narnia's best-known figure via 'The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe'; KING requires knowing Aslan rules Narnia or that the children become kings and queens.
Mufasa is the reigning king in The Lion King and is a lion; both sides are immediate for anyone who knows the film.
Simba is the lion cub who becomes king in The Lion King; the film title itself carries both words.

pairs.pair_note: MUFASA and SIMBA are both clean (same film); JUNGLE rides one universal idiom; THRONE and CROWN are king-side words with only a heraldic reach to the lion.

hints.reason: A tom is a male cat in plain English and Tom is the cartoon cat; MOUSE arrives through his nemesis Jerry, a widely known pairing.
Jerry is the Tom and Jerry mouse; CAT follows from his cartoon rival, a pairing most US adults know.
Cheese is the classic mouse bait; it says nothing about a cat.
Paws are a cat staple; mice do have paws but it is not a natural association for the mouse, so the second side needs prompting.
Click is the computer-mouse sense; there is no cat sense of click.
Whiskers are the cat's signature, and mice are also drawn and described by their whiskers (twitching whiskers, cartoon mice); natural to both animals.
Mousetrap is immediate; calling a cat a 'trap' for mice is an explanation, not a connection, and 'cat trap' is not a compound.
The cat is the chaser and the mouse the chased in the universal 'cat and mouse' chase; the association is natural to both words.

pairs.pair_note: CHASE is the most natural plain-sense hint; TOM and JERRY are one cartoon idea; WHISKERS passes as a shared animal feature; CHEESE, CLICK and TRAP are mouse-only.

hints.reason: Judged as compounds: 'Black Knight' (Arthurian legend, Monty Python, the Marvel character) on one side and 'black as night' / 'black night' on the other; both are established phrases.
'Knight in shining armor' is immediate; stars shining at night is a soft reach and 'shining night' is not a compound.
Night + mare makes nightmare; a mare is a horse, the knight's mount and the shape of the chess knight, so KNIGHT is a solid second reach.
Dark is the plain property of night, and 'The Dark Knight' (Batman) is a household title.
Armor is knight equipment with no night sense.
Owls are the nocturnal emblem of night; nothing links them to knights.

pairs.pair_note: DARK and BLACK both work through a famous Knight compound plus a plain night sense; MARE passes on the nightmare compound; ARMOR and OWL are one-sided.

hints.reason: Bats and spiders (with their cobwebs) are both standard Halloween decorations; the holiday is natural to each word.
Bats hang upside down and spiders hang from their threads; both are plain-sense and direct.
Web is the spider's signature; bats do not reach it.
Judged as compounds: Batman and Spider-Man, two of the most famous superheroes in the US; each is a direct hit.
Spiders are the archetypal creepy-crawly and bats are a stock creepy creature of the night; a mood word, but natural to both.
Bats live in caves and 'Batcave' is famous; cave spiders exist but are a stretch for the spider side.
Bats have wings; spiders do not.

pairs.pair_note: MAN (Batman / Spider-Man) and HANG are both clean; HALLOWEEN and CREEPY are natural shared associations; WEB and WINGS are one-sided.

hints.reason: Witch is a top Halloween icon and the black cat is a canonical Halloween image; natural to both.
Thackery Binx is the black cat cursed by the Sanderson witches in Hocus Pocus (1993); real, but the name is known mainly to fans of that film.
Broom is the witch's vehicle; cats have no claim on it.
Salem is the town of the witch trials and the talking black cat in Sabrina the Teenage Witch; two genuinely separate routes.
Sabrina the Teenage Witch is well known; CAT comes only from remembering her cat Salem.
A familiar is a witch's animal spirit in the occult sense, and the archetypal familiar is a cat; the everyday 'well-known' sense may distract some players.
Black cat is immediate, and black is the witch's colour (black hat, black robes, black magic); a natural easy hint for both.

pairs.pair_note: SALEM has two independent routes; FAMILIAR is a smart plain-sense hint; HALLOWEEN and BLACK are natural easy hints; BINX is accurate but niche.

hints.reason: Treasure is gold; fish do not come up.
Fishbowl is immediate; there is no 'gold bowl' compound, so GOLD arrives only by routing through 'goldfish bowl'.
Gold nugget is the first sense; 'fish nugget' is a real but minor frozen-food term that few US players would produce.
Fish scales are direct; weighing gold on scales is a real image (assayers, gold rush) but needs a nudge.
The hint literally contains both target words.
Gold rush is clear; there is no fish compound with rush.

Judged as compounds: Goldfinger (the Bond film) is broadly known; 'fish finger' is the British term for a fish stick, which most US adults recognise even if they do not use it, so FISH is a solid if slightly foreign reach.

pairs.pair_note: FINGER is the one hint that compounds on both sides; SCALES, BOWL and NUGGET each need a second step on the gold or fish side; GOLDFISH is disqualified.

hints.reason: Egg roll and spring roll are both everyday menu items.
A chick hatches from an egg; chicks are a spring/Easter symbol and 'spring chicken' is an idiom, a solid second reach.
A coil is a spring; eggs do not coil.
Yolk is pure egg; nothing on the spring side.
Scrambled eggs are immediate; no spring sense.
Easter eggs are iconic and Easter is the spring holiday.
Eggs sit in nests (and 'nest egg'); nesting happens in spring but that is seasonal background rather than a direct link.

pairs.pair_note: ROLL and EASTER are clean two-way hints and CHICK is a good third; COIL, YOLK and SCRAMBLE are one-sided.

hints.reason: A doubloon is a Spanish gold coin and the word lives almost entirely in pirate stories; slightly bookish but well known.
Gold coin is immediate; the pirate's chest of coins is a natural image for the pirate side.
Parrot on the shoulder is pure pirate; no gold link.
Walking the plank is pirate-only.
Pirate booty is immediate; booty means plunder, which implies gold only loosely.
Gold tooth is a stock phrase and the gold-toothed pirate is a stereotype; the pirate side depends on that one image.
Gold medal is direct; pirates do not win medals.
Treasure means gold in the popular imagination and pirate treasure is the archetype.

pairs.pair_note: TREASURE and DOUBLOON are both clean; COIN and TOOTH pass on natural pirate imagery; PARROT, PLANK and MEDAL are one-sided.

hints.reason: The hint literally contains both target words.
Fish tank is direct; no dog sense.
Dog bowl and fishbowl are both everyday phrases.
Fetch is a dog game; fish do not play it.
The dog is the archetypal pet and 'pet fish' is an everyday phrase; natural to both.
Dog bone is immediate and fish bones / fishbone are everyday.

pairs.pair_note: Three natural plain-sense hints; DOGFISH is disqualified; TANK and FETCH are one-sided.

hints.reason: Wolf pack is direct; there is no moon sense.
'Cry wolf' is a common idiom; MOON only arrives if the player pictures a wolf crying at the moon, and 'cry moon' is not a compound.
Full moon is immediate; WOLF follows only through the werewolf idea, which rides on the moon side.
The moon belongs to the night, and the wolf is culturally a creature of the night (howling in the dark, werewolf lore); natural to both.
Wolves howl, and 'howl at the moon' is a stock phrase.

pairs.pair_note: HOWL is the clean two-way hint and NIGHT is a natural shared setting; CRY and FULL each lean on one side; PACK is wolf-only.

hints.reason: The queen is a chess piece; chess has no ice sense.
Cold is the property of ice; the 'ice queen' idiom for an aloof woman is the only route to QUEEN, and that route goes through the other target rather than a 'cold queen' compound.
Arendelle is the kingdom in Frozen ruled by the ice-powered Queen Elsa; accurate, but the name is known mainly to Frozen fans and parents.
Elsa from Frozen has ice magic and is crowned Queen of Arendelle; a household name.
Ice cube is direct; nothing regal about a cube.
Snow sits next to ice; 'Snow Queen' (Andersen, Narnia, Frozen's source) is a known title, a solid second reach.
Frozen is the plain state of ice and the Disney film whose heroine becomes queen; the film is broadly known.

pairs.pair_note: ELSA and FROZEN are both clean (one film); SNOW passes via the Snow Queen title; ARENDELLE is correct but moderate recognizability; CHESS and CUBE are one-sided.

hints.reason: 'Blue moon' is a common idiom and the ocean is the archetypal blue thing; both sides are direct.
Ocean floor is a set phrase; 'moon floor' is not.
The moon's gravitational pull drives the ocean's tides, but both words need that explanation; PULL alone is abstract.
Tides belong to the ocean and are commonly known to be caused by the moon.
'The deep' is the ocean; the moon is not described as deep.
Craters are the moon's surface feature; no ocean sense.

pairs.pair_note: TIDE is excellent and BLUE is a natural colour hint for both; PULL is the tide idea without the word; the rest are one-sided.
